observations.statement: akhzar (H0393) applied to a non-human referent -- serpent venom ('the cruel venom of asps,' Deut 32:33) -- and to God's own untamable strength ('no one is so fierce that he dares stir him up,' Job 41:10, of Leviathan/God-language). Morph HAamsa (adjective, masc sing) both times. Neither occurrence describes a human moral agent.

akhzari (H0394) as an adjective (HAamsa throughout) describing human or cosmic agents defined by the explicit absence of mercy -- the Day of the Lord itself (Isa 13:9), a messenger sent as punishment (Prov 17:11), an enemy nation (Jer 30:14's 'merciless foe'), and armed raiders 'cruel and have no mercy' (Jer 6:23, 50:42, identical phrase in both).

akhzari's sixth occurrence is a deliberate paradox stated as its own proverb: 'the mercy of the wicked is cruel' (Prov 12:10) -- the wicked's gentlest disposition still qualifies as cruelty. Contrasted in the same verse with 'whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast.'

akhzariyyut (H0395) is morph HNcfsa -- an abstract NOUN, unlike H0393/H0394's adjective form (HAamsa) for the same root -- confirming this is the abstract-quality form ('cruelty, fierceness') rather than a description applied to a person or thing. Its one occurrence names 'wrath' itself as cruel ('wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming,' Prov 27:4) -- the quality attributed to an emotion, not an agent.

aritz (H6184) overwhelmingly naming human oppressors/adversaries from the position of the sufferer asking to be delivered from them -- Job's plea 'redeem me from the hand of the ruthless,' David's 'a band of ruthless men seeks my life,' Jeremiah's 'redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless,' and foreign-nation oppressors (Isa 25:3-5, 29:5/20, Ezek 28:7, 31:12).

Three of aritz's 15 occurrences render as 'warrior' (Jer 20:11), 'tyrant' (Isa 49:25), and 'oppressors' (Job 27:13) instead of 'ruthless.' The meaning block itself carries two poles -- 'awe-inspiring, terror-striking, awesome' (positive/divine register) alongside 'ruthless' (negative/human register) -- and these three surface divergences are exactly where the split shows up as a real usage distinction, not lexicographic hedging.

Jer 20:11's occurrence applies aritz to THE LORD HIMSELF as protector -- 'the Lord is with me as a dread warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble' -- using the meaning block's positive 'awe-inspiring/terror-striking' pole rather than the negative 'ruthless' pole that dominates every other occurrence. This is not an edge case to fold into the majority reading: it shows the same word genuinely carries two opposite moral valences (terrifying-oppressor vs. terrifying-protector) depending only on whose side the referent is on, exactly the same pattern already found for H1792/H1794 (dakha) in family F_violence_wound.

morph reviewed across H6184: singular (HAamsa) for individual referents (a tyrant, a warrior, a wicked man), plural (HAampa) for groups (ruthless men, ruthless nations' inhabitants), and construct plural (HAampc) specifically in the superlative idiom 'the most ruthless OF the nations' (Ezek 28:7, 31:12) -- ordinary grammatical number/construct-state variation tracking the referent, not a distinct sense.

This family's core finding -- cruelty defined by the explicit absence of mercy ('cruel and have no mercy,' 'the mercy of the wicked is cruel') and attributed almost entirely to an external agent/adversary rather than self-examined -- is structurally the opposite of the guilt subgroup's self-recognition pattern ('he realizes his guilt') and closer to family F_violence_wound's oppressor-vocabulary (chamas, dakha) than to the sin/guilt/transgression cluster of families this cluster is otherwise dominated by.
